questions.question: Describe the stages in the birth of a star, from a nebula to a stable star.
questions.expected_answer: A nebula is a cloud of mostly hydrogen gas and dust. A denser region (possibly triggered by a shock wave) begins to collapse under its own gravity. As the gas falls inwards it speeds up, collides and heats up, and the clump spins and forms a protostar surrounded by a disc. The protostar keeps contracting and its core heats up until about 10 million °C, when nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium begins. The energy released creates outward pressure that balances gravity, and the star becomes stable.

questions.question: Explain the difference between nuclear fusion and burning.
questions.expected_answer: Burning is a chemical reaction in which atoms rearrange and combine with oxygen; the nuclei do not change and no new elements are formed. Nuclear fusion is a nuclear reaction in which light nuclei (hydrogen) join to form a heavier nucleus (helium), producing a new element and converting a small amount of mass into a very large amount of energy, millions of times more than burning the same mass.

questions.question: Explain why a protostar is not yet a true star, and what happens if the collapsing clump has too little mass.
questions.expected_answer: A protostar glows because it is heated by contraction, but nuclear fusion of hydrogen has not yet started in its core; a true star shines by fusion with outward pressure balancing gravity. If the clump has less than about 8% of the Sun's mass, its core never reaches the temperature needed for hydrogen fusion, and it becomes a brown dwarf that glows faintly and cools.
